posts.metaDescription: Two different grading systems are in use, one traditional and one laboratory. Sellers mix them. Here is what each name actually means.
posts.excerpt: Two completely different systems are in use, one traditional and one laboratory. Sellers mix them deliberately.
posts.body:
Two completely different systems are in use for grading saffron, one traditional and one laboratory.

Sellers mix them, and the mixture is where the confusion lives.

## System one: what part of the stigma

The traditional Kashmiri names describe the physical cut. What part of the flower ended up in the tin.

- Mongra is the deep-red stigma tips only, separated from the yellow style.
- Lacha includes the red part plus some of the yellow style still attached.
- Zarda, also called Gucchi, is the whole stigma including the full yellow portion.

Each step down includes more yellow style. The style is part of the flower, so this is not adulteration. It is simply less of the part that carries the colour and aroma, and more of the part that does not.

That is why Mongra costs more per gram. You are buying a higher proportion of the working material, and the sorting that produces it throws away weight the seller could otherwise have sold.

The separation is done by hand, one flower at a time. Each crocus carries three stigmas, so a kilogram of Mongra takes roughly 150,000 flowers and more than a hundred hours of sorting.

## Why the tip matters

The red stigma tip is where the compounds sit. Crocin for colour, picrocrocin for taste, safranal for aroma.

Weight made up of yellow style is weight that does not do much in your pan. Buy a gram of Zarda and a gram of Mongra and you have bought two different amounts of working saffron, whatever the scale says.

This is also why cheap saffron often looks like a bargain and cooks like a disappointment. Nothing was faked. The ratio was different.

Against Lacha, Mongra gives 20-30% more colour per gram. In a pot of Kahwa or a Zafrani Pulao that is a deep gold against a pale yellow tint.

Ours is Mongra, tips only, and the tins are on the [products page](/products).

## System two: the laboratory categories

ISO 3632 is a separate axis entirely. It sorts saffron into categories by measured chemistry rather than by which part of the flower was used.

Category I requires, roughly, crocin at a minimum around 190 for filaments, picrocrocin above 70, safranal between 20 and 50, and moisture at 12 percent maximum. Published sources quote the crocin floor as both 190 and 200, because filament and powder thresholds differ.

The key point is that this system does not care what the cut is called. It measures what is there.

## The two systems are not interchangeable

A cut name tells you what part of the flower is in the tin. A category tells you how the contents tested.

You can have Mongra that tests as Category I. You can, in principle, have Mongra that tests lower, if it was dried badly or stored badly or is simply from a weaker crop. The cut does not guarantee the chemistry, because drying and storage happen after the sorting.

It works the other way too. A lower cut with a lot of style in it is carrying dead weight that a chemical test on the whole sample will notice.

This is why a serious answer to "how good is this saffron" needs both. The cut, and the three numbers.

## Where Negin fits

Negin is an Iranian and Afghan trade grade: whole, thick red stigmas cut with no yellow style, often with the three threads still joined. Super Negin is a further selection of the longest and thickest.

Neither is an ISO category and neither is a Kashmiri grade. Kashmir uses Mongra and Lacha. Spain has a third vocabulary again, set out in [what origin actually tells you](/blog/origins-compared/).

A listing saying "Super Negin Kashmiri Mongra" is stacking two regions' vocabularies, which usually describes a look rather than an origin.

## "Super Negin Mongra Category I"

You will see strings like that on listings, and it is worth recognising what is happening.

Three grading vocabularies have been stacked into one phrase. Two of them describe roughly the same thing from different traditions, and the third is a laboratory result. Stacking them looks like three separate guarantees. It is closer to one and a half.

It is not necessarily dishonest. It is imprecise in a direction that flatters the product, which is the most common kind of imprecision in this market.

## Powder is a separate question

None of the cut names in this article survive grinding, because a cut is a visible fact about a thread and a powder has none. We sell whole stigmas only, and [saffron powder against threads](/blog/powder-or-threads/) sets out what you give up, what you gain, and what a powder seller would have to show you.

## Why the systems got mixed

The two vocabularies come from different places and were never designed to sit together.

The cut names are old, local and descriptive. They come from people sorting stigmas by hand and needing a word for what was in each pile. The ISO categories are recent, international and analytical. They come from laboratories needing a comparable measure for trade.

Sellers reach for both because each answers a question the other cannot, and because more grading words look like more assurance. The result is listings where the vocabulary is doing marketing work rather than describing anything.

## What to ask instead

Skip the adjectives and ask four things:

- Is this stigma tips only, or does it include the style?
- Which laboratory tested it?
- What were the crocin, picrocrocin and safranal values?
- What is the lot number on this tin?

Those four answers describe the product completely. Any grade name is a shorthand for some part of them, and shorthand is where the room to mislead lives.

posts.title: Why We Do Not Make Health Claims
posts.metaTitle: Why We Do Not Make Health Claims
posts.metaDescription: Two regulators prohibit a food seller from advertising a food as acting on a disease. Here is what they say, and what we say instead.
posts.excerpt: We sell saffron as food. We do not tell you what it does to your body, and there are rules behind that rather than coyness.
posts.body:
We sell saffron as food. We do not tell you what it does to your body, and we are not going to start.

That is a choice with rules behind it, not coyness, and it is worth setting out plainly because almost every other saffron seller you will read does the opposite.

## Two markets, one rule, two vocabularies

Most of what we send goes to the Gulf and to India. Both regulate what a food seller may say.

India's Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018, at regulation 10(1):

"no claims shall be made which refer to the suitability of the food for use in the prevention, alleviation, treatment or cure of a disease, disorder or particular physiological condition unless specifically permitted under any other regulations made under Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006"

The UAE standard on permitted health and nutrition claims, at clause 11.1.4, prohibits:

"Claims show that a food can be used in the prevention, alleviation, treatment or cure of a disease, disorder or particular physiological condition."

Two jurisdictions, near-identical wording, same effect. A food is not permitted to be advertised as acting on a disease or a physiological condition.

A note on that second source, because this article would be a poor advertisement for its own argument otherwise. The operative UAE standard is GSO 2333, and it sits behind a paywall we have not paid. What we quoted is the 2018 final draft issued by the Emirates Authority for Standardization and Metrology and notified to the World Trade Organization, which is public. It is a draft. We are citing it as a draft and not pretending it is the settled text.

## This page counts

It would be convenient to treat a blog as different from a label. The Indian regulation closes that off in its definitions, where an advertisement includes publicity or representation made by print, electronic media, internet or website.

So an article on this domain is covered. This one included.

## Both regimes work from a list

Neither rule is only a prohibition. Both are built the same way: a set of claims is permitted, conditions attach to each, and anything outside the set needs prior approval from the authority.

We went looking for saffron in both permitted lists. We did not find it in the parts we were able to read.

That is the honest form of the finding and we are going to leave it in that form. We could not read the paywalled UAE standard, and one table in the draft did not extract cleanly. So the accurate statement is that we found no approved claim for saffron, not that none exists.

## Research exists, and it is still not ours to repeat

There is published research on saffron. We know it is there. We are not going to summarise it, link it, or tell you what it looked at.

Two reasons, and the second is the real one.

The first is that none of it is about our tins. A study is about the material a laboratory was given, under conditions someone else chose.

The second is that a summary of research, published by the company selling the product, is not a neutral act. It becomes a representation about the food we sell, which is precisely what the two rules above address. Adding "this is not a claim" underneath does not change what the page is doing.

The version of this article that reads "here is what studies have examined" is the version we decided not to write. It would have brought traffic. It would also have been us saying, in a longer way, the thing we are telling you we do not say.

## What we do say

Refusing one kind of statement is only worth something if we make the other kind properly.

Everything we assert about our saffron is a measurable property of the material, and every one of them has a document behind it:

- The three ISO 3632 values, crocin, picrocrocin and safranal, with the figures rather than the category alone.
- The laboratory that measured them and its accreditation.
- The lot number, so the report attaches to the tin you are holding.
- The cut, and what that word does and does not mean.
- Where it was grown, named down to the fields.

Those are claims we can be held to. If one is wrong, a test settles it, and our purity guarantee is written so that a failed test costs us the sale and the price of the test.

A claim about what saffron does inside a person cannot be settled that way by us, which is the other reason not to make it.

## Where this is written down

None of this is new policy invented for an article. Our [terms](/terms) already carry it, and have from the start:

"Nothing on this site is medical advice. We make no claim that saffron treats, prevents or cures any condition. Speak to a doctor before using saffron medicinally, particularly if you are pregnant or taking medication."

That paragraph and this article say the same thing. This one just shows the regulations behind it.

## The short version

We sell a spice. We will tell you what is in the tin, who measured it, and what the numbers were.

We will not tell you what it will do for you, because two regulators say a food seller may not, because we could not verify an approved claim in either permitted list, and because a company summarising research about its own product is making a claim whatever it calls the paragraph.

If you want to know what saffron does in the body, ask someone who is not selling it to you.

posts.title: Kashmiri, Iranian and Spanish Saffron: What Origin Actually Tells You
posts.metaTitle: Kashmiri vs Iranian vs Spanish Saffron
posts.metaDescription: Origin is a weak predictor of quality and a strong predictor of price, vocabulary and supply chain. What the comparison survives, and what it does not.
posts.excerpt: The quality comparison between Kashmiri, Iranian and Spanish saffron does not survive being checked. What origin does tell you is which grading vocabulary you are reading.
posts.body:
Kashmiri, Iranian, Spanish. Three labels, and the question everyone asks is which one is best.

We sell one of them. So read our answer with that in front of you, and know that the question does not survive being checked anyway.

## Our conclusion, at the top where you can weigh it

We grow saffron in Pampore and we sell it. Any article from us ranking the three origins is marketing in a lab coat, so here is where this ends up before you read the argument.

Origin is a weak predictor of quality. It is a strong predictor of price, of vocabulary, and of the supply chain a tin came down.

What tells you the quality of the saffron in your hand is the lab report on that lot. Not the country on the label, and not ours either.

## Iran grows most of the world's saffron

The FAO puts Iran at 85 to 90 percent of world production.

FAO's own heritage-site page for the qanat-based saffron system in Gonabad says over 90 percent. We are not going to pick whichever number flatters this page. The honest version is that Iran grows the overwhelming majority, and the same organisation reports the exact share differently in two places.

That is the setting for everything below. Most saffron in the world is Iranian, and a great deal of it is very good.

## The quality comparison does not survive checking

We went looking for crocin ranges by origin so this article could put them side by side. We are not going to publish any, and the reason is worth more than the table would have been.

The figures that circulate come almost entirely from sellers. They disagree with each other, and each one disagrees in the direction of whoever published it.

The published research does not support the comparison either. A 2021 metabolomics study examined saffron from Greece, Italy, Morocco, Iran, India, Afghanistan and Kashmir, and reported that the crocins were not among the compounds that significantly differentiated the samples. It found differences between origins. Crocin was not where they sat.

So the number people argue about in origin comparisons is not the number that separates these origins, at least not in the work that went looking.

## What Spain actually is

Spain is one of the largest exporters of saffron in the world and it is nowhere near one of the largest growers. Both things are true at once, because a large share of what leaves Spain arrived in Spain first.

This is not a rumour with a grudge behind it. A 2016 study in Food Chemistry fingerprinted saffron by liquid chromatography and high resolution mass spectrometry, and separated, on chemistry alone, saffron grown and packed in Spain under the protected designation from saffron packed in Spain of unknown origin and sold as Spanish saffron.

Read what that does and does not say. It does not identify where the unknown-origin material was grown. It says that "Spanish saffron" on a label covers at least two different things, and that a laboratory can tell them apart when a shelf cannot.

If the shape of that is familiar, it is the same argument [we make about Kashmir](/blog/arithmetic-of-origin/), arriving from another country. This is not a Kashmiri problem or a Spanish one. It is what happens anywhere a place name is worth more per gram than the saffron is.

## Three vocabularies that do not convert

Each producing region grades saffron in its own language, and the languages describe different things.

- Kashmir uses Mongra, Lacha and Zarda. These describe the cut: how much of the yellow style is in the tin alongside the red stigma.
- Iran uses Sargol, Negin and Pushal, which describe the cut and the appearance of the thread together.
- The Spanish trade uses Coupe, Mancha, Rio and Sierra, ordered by colouring power.

None of these converts into another. A Coupe is not a Mongra with a Spanish accent. [Our article on grade names](/blog/grade-names/) sets out the Kashmiri system and where Negin actually belongs.

## The Spanish protected designation has no grades at all

This is the part that surprised us, and it is the most useful thing on this page.

Azafrán de La Mancha is a protected designation of origin. We read its specification. It does not define Coupe, or Rio, or Sierra. Those words do not appear in it, except where Rio and Sierra turn up inside the names of towns in the growing area.

What the PDO sets is a single standard rather than a ladder: colouring power above 200, aromatic power above 20, bitter power above 70, moisture and volatile matter below 11 percent, extraneous matter at or below 0.5 percent, and a minimum stigma to style length ratio of 2 to 1. Analysis follows UNE-ISO 3632-2.

So Coupe and Sierra are trade language, and Selecto is a shop label. Neither is the protected designation. A tin can carry any of those words and carry no PDO at all.

## Two numbers that are not the numbers you think

The figures in that specification look like figures you have seen elsewhere. They are not the same claims, and confusing them is the easiest mistake to make on this subject.

The PDO's colouring power floor of 200 is the PDO's own threshold for its own saffron. ISO 3632 Category I is a separate standard with its own floor, which published summaries give as either 190 or 200 for filaments, for reasons [set out here](/blog/read-lab-report/). Two numbers can be near each other and still be answering different questions.

The moisture limits differ outright. The PDO requires below 11 percent. ISO 3632 allows up to 12. Spanish PDO saffron is held to a tighter moisture limit than the international standard asks for, and that is a real difference rather than a marketing one.

## The same criticism lands on us

A listing reading "Super Negin Kashmiri Mongra" stacks an Iranian trade grade, a region and a Kashmiri cut into one phrase, and our grade names article takes that apart at length. The identical move happens with Spanish vocabulary. It also happens with ours, and we are not exempt because we wrote the criticism.

We call our saffron Mongra. That word describes a cut, stigma tips with the yellow style removed. It is accurate, and it is not a quality certificate. It does not tell you our crocin figure. It does not tell you which laboratory. It does not tell you the lot number on the tin in front of you.

## What origin does tell you

Origin is not useless. It is just not a measure of quality.

- Which grading vocabulary the seller is working in, and therefore which questions will make sense to them.
- Roughly what you should expect to pay, which is [its own subject](/blog/what-saffron-costs/).
- How much of the stuff exists. Kashmir's growing area is small and shrinking, and [the arithmetic](/blog/arithmetic-of-origin/) is unforgiving.
- Whether a legal protection exists and what it actually covers, which for Kashmir is [GI No. 635](/blog/gi-635/).

Not one of those is "this tin is better than that tin". All of them are worth knowing before you spend.

## The short version

Iran grows most of the world's saffron and much of it is excellent. Spain exports far more than it grows. Kashmir grows very little of the world total and has a great deal more sold under its name than it can possibly produce.

The origin on a tin tells you which vocabulary you are reading and roughly what you will pay. It does not tell you what is inside the tin.

For that there are three questions, and they work in every country on this page including ours. Which laboratory tested it. What were the three numbers. What is the lot number.

posts.title: Saffron Powder vs Threads: What You Can Actually Check
posts.metaDescription: Powder is not inferior saffron. It is unverifiable saffron. What you give up, where powder is genuinely better, and why grinding your own gets both.
posts.excerpt: Powder is not weaker saffron. It is saffron you cannot check, and every test on this site assumes a thread.
posts.body:
Powder is not weaker saffron. It is saffron you cannot check.

That is the whole argument, and it lands differently depending on what you are buying it for.

## We sell threads only, so read this knowing that

Worth saying before anything else. We sell whole stigmas. We do not sell powder and we are not planning to. So we have an interest in you preferring threads, and you should weigh what follows accordingly.

What we are not going to tell you is that powder is bad saffron. Plenty of good saffron is sold as powder, and at its best it is exactly what it says: good threads, ground, nothing else. The problem is not what powder can be. It is what powder can hide, and the fact that you have no way to separate the two in your kitchen.

## Every check you can run assumes a thread

Go through the tests on this site and notice what they have in common.

The [home purity tests](/blog/purity-tests/) work on structure and behaviour. The trumpet shape at one end of a real stigma. How the colour comes out of it in water. What the threads do when you rub them. Safflower, marigold petal and dyed corn silk get caught because they do not look like a stigma close up.

Grind all of that and every one of those tests stops working. There is no trumpet in a powder. There is no thread to rub. The water test tells you less, because you cannot see what is releasing the colour.

The [grade names](/blog/grade-names/) go the same way. Mongra, Lacha and Zarda describe how much yellow style is in the tin, and that is a visible fact about threads. In a powder it is invisible, and a powder made mostly of style still looks like saffron powder.

## The standard already treats them as two things

This is the part people miss. ISO 3632 does not apply one set of thresholds to saffron. It sets different ones for filaments and for powder.

That is part of why published figures for Category I vary depending on which summary you read, as [reading a lab report](/blog/read-lab-report/) sets out. The standard is not being vague. Different summaries are quoting different rows.

The useful version for a buyer: a powder that passes has been measured against powder thresholds. Category I on a jar of powder and Category I on a tin of threads are not the same sentence.

## What is left when the checks are gone

If you cannot examine the thing, you are left with the seller and the paperwork.

That is not nothing. A lab report with a lot number that matches the jar in your hand is worth more than any test you can run at a kitchen table. It is just that with threads you have the report and your own eyes, and with powder you have only the report.

So the question to ask about a powder is not whether it is good. It is what would prove it. If the answer comes back as a brand name, you have nothing.

## Where powder is genuinely better

The other side, because there is one.

- It disperses. Powder goes evenly through a dough, a batter or a dry rub in a way whole threads never will.
- It extracts faster. When a dish is short on time, or has no liquid to bloom in, ground saffron gets there sooner.
- It is consistent. Every spoonful of a mixed powder carries the same amount, which matters in baking, where you are not tasting as you go and correcting.
- Nobody is picking threads out of it. In a smooth dish, visible threads are a texture some people do not want.

Those are real advantages and none of them is solved by using threads better.

## Grind them yourself

The way to get both is dull and it works. Buy threads, check them, grind what the dish needs.

[How much saffron to actually use](/blog/how-much-to-use/) covers the mechanics: a pinch ground with a little sugar or salt extracts faster and more completely, and the grinding medium stops the threads sticking to the mortar.

Grind small and grind often. A ground batch loses aroma faster than a whole one, because you have made a great deal more surface for it to leave from. Powder is a thing to make on the day, not a way to store saffron.

The point is the order. You do the checking once, on the threads, before anything is ground. After that the powder in your mortar has a history you watched.

## What we would ask a powder seller

The same questions as anything else, plus one.

- Which laboratory tested it, and is the lot number on the jar?
- Were the values measured against the powder thresholds or the filament ones?
- What was ground, in grade terms, and how would a buyer know?
- Is there anything else in the jar, including anti-caking agents?

The last one is the extra, and it is the reason powder needs its own conversation. A powder can legitimately contain something that is not saffron and still be labelled honestly. A tin of whole threads cannot.

## The short version

Buy threads when you want to be able to check what you bought, which for most people paying saffron prices is the entire point.

Use powder when the dish genuinely needs it, and make it yourself where you can, from threads you have already looked at.

Powder is not a lesser product. It is a product that moves all of the trust onto the seller, and this is a market where that has not gone well.

posts.title: How to Store Saffron So It Is Still Worth What You Paid
posts.metaDescription: Saffron does not spoil, it fades. Light, heat, air and moisture in order of damage, and why the fridge is usually the wrong answer.
posts.excerpt: Saffron does not spoil. It fades. Most of what people call bad saffron is good saffron stored badly.
posts.body:
Saffron does not spoil. It fades.

Most of what people call bad saffron is good saffron stored badly, and the fading is not evenly distributed across the three things you paid for.

## The four enemies, in order

Light does the most damage, then heat, then air, then moisture.

- Light breaks down the compounds that carry colour and aroma. A clear jar on a shelf is the worst common storage choice.
- Heat accelerates everything. Above the stove is convenient and wrong.
- Air means slow oxidation and, more immediately, the escape of the volatile compounds that give saffron its smell.
- Moisture is the one that does structural damage, and saffron will pull it out of the room if you let it.

An airtight tin, kept dark and cool and closed, deals with all four. That is why saffron is sold in tins rather than clear jars, and it is why the tin is worth keeping rather than decanting into something prettier.

## Safranal goes first

Of the three measured compounds, safranal is the volatile one. It is what you smell.

That means aroma degrades before colour does. A tin that has been open on a warm shelf for a year can still throw good colour into rice while smelling of very little. People read that as "it still works", and it does, partly. You are getting the crocin and losing the perfume.

The practical signal: if you open the tin and it smells faint, the safranal has gone even though the crocin may be largely intact. Expect colour and less scent, and expect to be slightly disappointed in a dish where the aroma was the point.

## Why moisture is the expensive one

ISO 3632 caps moisture at 12 percent for a reason.

Saffron left in a humid kitchen takes water out of the air. That adds weight you already paid for as saffron, softens the threads, and moves the batch towards the edge of the standard it was tested against. A tin that tested comfortably inside Category I when it left the lab is not guaranteed to still be there after a year above a kettle.

This is the one form of degradation that changes a measurable number rather than just a smell.

## Why the fridge is usually wrong

This is the mistake we get asked about most.

A fridge is cool and dark, which sounds ideal. It is also humid, and every time you take the tin out, warm room air meets a cold tin and condensation forms inside it. You have introduced the one enemy that does the most structural harm, repeatedly.

Unless you can guarantee a genuinely airtight container and you are not opening it often, a cool dark cupboard beats a fridge. A freezer has the same condensation problem with more temperature swing per use.

## If you cook somewhere humid

Most of our orders go to the Gulf and to India. The humidity problem is different in each, and the one people expect is usually backwards.

An air-conditioned flat is a dehumidified flat. Cooling air makes water condense out of it, so a unit running through a Dubai summer is pulling moisture out of the room as a side effect. A closed cupboard in that flat is often drier than a kitchen in Kerala or Mumbai in July with the windows open.

So the Gulf risk is not the flat with the air conditioning on. It is the flat with it off: a place shut up for a month, a kitchen running on a generator, a store cupboard on a balcony. Heat and damp arrive together and the tin is the only thing between them and the saffron.

Monsoon India is the harder case, because nothing is taking the water back out. The air holds it for weeks, and a lid resting rather than seated is enough.

The answer does not change. It just matters more. Seat the lid properly. Do not decant. Do not leave the tin open on the counter while the dish cooks and come back to it when you are done.

People keep a few grains of rice in with ground spices to hold the damp off. Do not do it with saffron. Rice is dusty, it grinds against the threads every time the tin moves, and it takes on the aroma you paid for. A food-safe silica sachet in an outer box does no harm if it makes you feel better, and it is unnecessary if the tin seals.

A tin kept badly in a wet kitchen does not announce itself. It just needs more threads for the same dish, which is the slow way of paying twice. [How much saffron to actually use](/blog/how-much-to-use/) covers what a working pinch looks like.

## Freezing, and why it does not help

The question we get is whether a freezer beats a cupboard in a wet climate.

It does not, for the reason the fridge does not. Every time the tin comes out, warm room air meets cold metal and water forms inside it. Do that once a month and you have repeated the damage you were trying to avoid, at a lower temperature.

There is a version that works, and it is worth being straight about it. A sealed tin, frozen once, brought fully back to room temperature before it is opened, and then not put back, is fine. That is a way to hold saffron you are not going to touch for a year. It is not a way to store saffron you cook with, because the cooking is the part that breaks it.

Most people will not thaw a tin properly every single time. A dry closed cupboard costs nothing and asks nothing of you. Use the cupboard.

## What to keep it in

The tin it arrived in is the right container for three dull reasons. It is opaque, it seals, and it is about the size of what is inside it. Most alternatives fail one of those.

- Clear glass fails the first one, and light is top of the list. It is the common mistake because it is the one that looks best on a shelf.
- Amber or opaque glass with a proper gasket is genuinely fine. A dark sealed jar in a closed cupboard does everything the tin does. If you own one and prefer it, use it.
- Foil is not storage. It is how loose saffron comes off a market stall. It creases, it tears at the fold and it does not seal, so it handles light and ignores air and damp. Move it out the day it arrives.
- Stainless steel seals well, blocks all light, and does not hold smells. The drawback is real: you cannot see the level, so it goes to the back of a cupboard and stays there.
- Plastic takes on the smell of whatever it held before and gives some of it back. A clip box that had cumin in it is not a saffron container. Threads cling to the sides with static as well, and you lose a few each time.
- Vacuum containers are more than the job needs. Air is third on the list, not first, and a closed lid was already dealing with it.

The size point is the one people miss. A large jar holding a small amount of saffron is holding a large amount of air against it. The tin was sized for what came in it.

So: opaque, sealing, no bigger than it needs to be. The most common way a good tin of saffron gets worse is a container chosen for how it looks.


## Realistic shelf life

Stored properly, in a closed tin, dark and cool and dry, saffron stays good for a long time. It does not become unsafe. It becomes weaker.

What changes, roughly in order: aroma first, then taste, then colour last. A tin several years old and well kept will still colour a dish. It will smell like a shadow of a fresh one.

Properly stored, saffron keeps 2-3 years without spoiling. It does not go off, it fades. Safranal drops first, so aroma weakens before colour does. For full aroma, use it within 12 months of harvest.

Those are guides, not a use-by date. Storage decides the outcome more than the calendar does.

## Buy the size you will use

There is a practical consequence to all of this.

A large tin bought once and opened weekly for three years will spend most of its life degrading. A smaller tin finished in a few months spends most of its life sealed. The price per gram is better on the larger tin, and the saffron you actually cook with may be better from the smaller one.

That is not a sales argument in our favour, since the bigger tins are the better margin per gram for a buyer. It is just true.

## What this means for a return

This connects directly to our [Returns Policy](/returns-policy).

We will replace a tin that arrived damaged, and we will replace an unopened tin returned with the seal intact within 7 days. We cannot replace saffron that has lost its aroma after being stored open, warm, or in the light, because that is degradation after delivery rather than a fault in what we sent.

That is not us being difficult. There is no way to distinguish a weak batch from a well-treated one after the fact without a lab, and the compounds involved leave on their own schedule regardless of who is at fault.

## Where people actually keep it

The three places saffron usually ends up are all wrong, and all three are chosen for convenience.

A spice rack beside the hob gets heat every time you cook. A clear jar in a window looks attractive and destroys aroma fastest of anything on this list. A drawer that also holds the kettle or the dishwasher vent gets steam.

The right place is dull: a closed cupboard away from the cooking, at room temperature, with the tin shut. It is not a storage solution anyone photographs.

## The short version

Keep it in the tin. Keep the tin closed, dark, cool and dry. Not the fridge, not above the stove, not in a clear jar on the counter.

Do that and the saffron you paid for is the saffron you cook with in two years' time.

posts.title: How Much Saffron to Actually Use
posts.metaTitle: How Much Saffron to Use per Dish
posts.metaDescription: Most recipes over-specify saffron by a factor of two or more, and over-steeping makes it bitter rather than stronger.
posts.excerpt: Most recipes over-specify saffron by a factor of two or more, and over-steeping makes it bitter, not stronger.
posts.body:
Most recipes over-specify saffron by a factor of two or more.

Over-steeping does not fix a small amount either. Past a point it turns the result harsh rather than stronger.

## Threads per serving

As a working guide for good Mongra grade, per serving:

- Rice for 4-6 people: 20-25 threads
- One cup of milk or tea: 8-10 threads
- Desserts, per 500ml base: 15-20 threads

A strong Category I lot needs fewer threads than the same weight of Category III. Thread size also varies with the cut, so treat these as a starting point rather than a rule.

If you want the specific quantities we use, they are written into each of our [recipes](/recipes), measured for the grade we sell.

## Blooming

Saffron does not give up much if you throw it in dry.

Warm liquid, not boiling. Boiling water drives off the aroma you are trying to extract, and safranal is the compound that leaves first. Warm milk, warm water, warm stock, depending on the dish.

Give it 10 to 20 minutes. The liquid turns deep gold and the threads stay red. Then use the liquid, threads and all, in the dish.

Choose the liquid to match what you are cooking. Milk for kheer and kesar doodh, water for rice, a spoonful of the dish's own stock for a savoury pot. The saffron carries into whatever it was bloomed in, so blooming in something that does not belong in the dish wastes part of it.

## Whole threads or ground

Grinding changes the result.

A pinch ground with a little sugar or salt before blooming extracts faster and more completely, which is useful when the dish is short on time. The grinding medium stops the threads simply sticking to the mortar.

Whole threads look better in a finished plate, and in a rice dish the visible red threads are part of the point. Choose per dish rather than by rule.

## When to add it

Late, in most cases.

Saffron added at the start of a long braise spends an hour losing aroma to the air. The colour survives that. The smell does not.

For rice, the bloomed liquid goes in at the point where the grain will absorb it rather than boil it away. For a curry or a stew, near the end. For milk-based drinks and desserts, off the heat or at a gentle simmer.

## Why more is not better

There is a point where extra saffron stops adding perfume and starts adding a bitter edge. It is not subtle when you cross it.

The same is true of steeping time. Twenty minutes in warm liquid gets you most of what is available. Two hours does not double it, and long steeping in hot liquid loses aroma out of the top of the pan while you wait.

If a dish is not tasting of saffron, the usual cause is that it was added dry, or added too early, not that the amount was too small. Increasing the amount to fix a technique problem is how people end up with an expensive, slightly harsh dinner.

## Cost per serving

This is the number worth doing, because it is not what people expect.

Saffron is expensive per gram and cheap per plate. A dish serving four takes a small pinch. Our 2g tin is AED 65 and does 15 to 20 servings of tea or rice.

Work it out per serving and saffron sits in the same range as many everyday spices used generously. The sticker price on the tin is what alarms people. The per-plate cost rarely does, and it is the only one that matters once the tin is in the cupboard.

## Grade changes the amount

A gram of Category I with a high crocin value goes further than a gram of a lower grade. That is the whole point of the number.

So a recipe written for unknown saffron will over-specify for good saffron and under-specify for weak. If you switch grade, expect to adjust, and adjust downwards when moving up in quality.

The same applies when you move from a cut with yellow style in it to tips only. You are getting more working material per pinch, so the pinch gets smaller.

## Storing what you did not use

Bloomed saffron liquid does not keep well. Make what the dish needs.

The threads themselves go back in the tin, closed, in a dark cupboard. Aroma is the first thing to leave a badly stored tin, which means poor storage quietly raises the amount you need for the same result, and you will not notice it happening.

If a tin that used to work at a small pinch now seems weak, look at where it has been living before increasing the amount. [How to store saffron](/blog/storing-saffron/) covers where it should be living.

## The short version

Less than the recipe says. Warm liquid, not boiling. Ten to twenty minutes. Use the liquid and the threads. Add it late.

Start at the low end and add next time. It is much easier to add saffron to the next batch than to take a harsh edge out of this one.

posts.title: Harvest Diary: This Season in Our Fields
posts.metaDescription: Dated photographs from one family field in Pampore during the three weeks the crop exists, and what this season actually yielded.
posts.excerpt: Photographs with dates on them, from our own fields, during the three weeks the crop exists.
posts.body:
Photographs with dates on them, from our own fields, during the three weeks the crop exists.

This post is written during the bloom and published during it. If you are reading it, the dates on the images are real.

## The window

Saffron gives you a few days.

The flowers come up almost overnight in autumn and each one is open for a short time. Miss the morning and the petals begin to go. The whole crop for the year comes off the fields inside a window measured in weeks, not months.

There is no second attempt. A field that is not picked on the right morning is not picked, and that portion of the year is gone. That is why every step of this is done by hand and at speed, and why the labour cost is what it is.

[YOUR PHOTO]

## Picking before the sun

Picking starts before dawn.

Sun and heat open the flowers fully and start driving off the volatile compounds, safranal first. A flower picked in the cool dark holds more of what you are growing it for than the same flower picked at midday.

So the fields fill before first light and the work is done in the cold, bent over, one flower at a time. Whole families come out for it, because the window does not wait and there is no machine that does this.

[YOUR PHOTO]

## Separating the stigmas

Every flower is opened and the three red stigmas are pulled out by hand.

This is indoor work, done sitting down, and it takes far longer than the picking. It is also where the grade is decided. Mongra means the red tips only, with the yellow style separated off and set aside. Doing that properly is slow, and doing it fast is how style ends up in the tin and a lower grade gets sold as a higher one.

160 to 180 flowers make one gram of dried saffron. That number stops being abstract when the flowers are in front of you in a basket and you are three hours into a pile that will not become very much.

[YOUR PHOTO]

## Drying

Drying sets the final quality and it is the easiest step to get wrong.

Under-dried saffron carries too much moisture, which fails the ISO 3632 limit of 12 percent maximum and pads the weight with water. It also will not keep, because moisture is what does structural damage in storage.

Over-dried saffron loses aroma. Safranal is volatile and heat takes it. You can dry a batch to a number that passes on moisture and still have ruined the smell getting there.

There is a narrow correct answer and it is reached by watching rather than by a timer.

[YOUR PHOTO]

## What can go wrong

Plenty, and it is worth saying so in a post like this.

Weather at the wrong moment shortens the window. Rain during the bloom damages flowers on the plant. A warm morning costs aroma before the pickers reach the row. A slow separating day means flowers sitting too long before their stigmas come out.

None of that is visible in a finished tin. It is visible in the lab numbers, months later, which is one reason we test rather than trusting a good-looking harvest.

## The rest of the year

Three weeks decide the crop, and the other forty-nine are not empty.

Corms are lifted, divided and replanted on a cycle, because Crocus sativus is sterile and every new plant comes from an existing one. Fields are weeded and watered. Drainage matters, because the plateau soil holds the crop only if the water moves through it.

None of that produces anything you can sell. It produces next year's three weeks, which is the only thing that does.

## What this season actually gave

[YOUR FIELD]

Write the real number here, in whatever unit is actually measured, and write it even if it is bad. Especially if it is bad.

Context worth including: the growers' association reported the 2025 season at 10 to 15 percent of normal, and the official production series for recent years do not agree with each other or with that figure. A single honest field number is worth more than any of them, because at least you know what it is measuring.

## Why it is done this way

Every slow step above has a reason, and the reasons are all the same reason.

Saffron is three compounds sitting in a small piece of plant material: crocin for colour, picrocrocin for taste, safranal for aroma. Every stage of the harvest is either protecting those compounds or losing them. Picking cold protects them. Separating quickly protects them. Drying carefully protects them. Heat, delay and rough handling lose them.

That is the whole craft. There is no clever technique that adds anything. There is only a series of chances to lose what the flower already made, and the work is in not taking them.

## Why this post exists

Anyone can buy a photograph of a saffron field. Nobody can buy this week in these fields.

That is the entire argument. We would rather show you the work, dated, including a bad year, than write another page about heritage. The land in Kashmir has fallen from 5,707 hectares in the late 1990s to about 3,665 as of 2025, and around 20,000 families still depend on this crop. What that looks like up close is a cold morning and a basket.
